title: Pub/Sub & Events
summary: Announce that something happened, and let whoever cares react — without anyone waiting.

goals.text: Why direct calls couple services together
The outbox pattern and replaying events

steps.title: Checkout calls everyone
body: When an order is placed, four other things must happen: send a confirmation email, reserve stock, record analytics, add loyalty points.
The order service calls each of them in turn and waits for every answer, so the shopper waits for all four — almost a second.

callout.text: Every new feature that cares about orders means changing, testing and redeploying the order service.

steps.title: Email is down, so nobody can buy
body: The email provider has an outage. The order service’s call to it fails — and because checkout waits on every call, checkout fails.
A confirmation email, which could easily have been sent ten minutes later, just stopped all sales.

callout.text: With direct calls, availability multiplies: four services at 99.9% each give checkout about 99.6%.

steps.title: Publish an event instead
body: The order service now saves the order and publishes one event — OrderPlaced — to a topic on an event bus, then answers the shopper straight away.
Email, inventory, analytics and loyalty each subscribe to the topic, and every one of them receives its own copy of the event.

callout.text: Common brokers: Kafka, Amazon SNS + SQS, Google Pub/Sub, RabbitMQ (fanout exchanges), Redis Streams.

steps.title: Queue or topic?
body: In the last lesson, each job went to one worker — a queue shares out work. A topic does the opposite: each event goes to every subscriber — it spreads news.
Real systems combine them: each subscribing service gets its own queue of events, shared by however many instances of that service are running.

card.title: Queue vs topic
lines: queue → each message to ONE consumer
topic → each message to EVERY subscriber

steps.title: New features just subscribe
body: The risk team wants to check every order for fraud. They build a service that subscribes to OrderPlaced — and that’s it.
The order service didn’t change, wasn’t redeployed, and doesn’t even know fraud checking exists. This is loose coupling.

callout.text: Publishers don’t know their subscribers. Teams can add reactions to events without coordinating releases.

steps.title: A subscriber is down? It catches up
body: Email is down again. This time checkout doesn’t notice: the event bus keeps email’s copies of the events in its subscription until it’s back.
When email recovers, it works through the backlog and every confirmation goes out — a little late, but none lost.

callout.text: Events are durable: a slow or broken subscriber delays only itself.

changes: + Its events wait in its subscription

steps.title: What events cost
body: Events decouple services, but the flow becomes harder to see: “what happens when an order is placed?” is now spread across five codebases.
Subscribers act a little later (eventual consistency), events can arrive twice or out of order, and debugging needs good tracing.

callout.text: Name events as facts in the past tense (OrderPlaced, PaymentFailed), and make every subscriber idempotent.

card.title: Events: the fine print
lines: who reacts to OrderPlaced? check 5 repos

steps.title: Case: saved, but never announced
body: The order service saves the order to its database, then publishes OrderPlaced. One day it crashes between those two steps: the order exists, but no event was sent. No email, no stock reserved, no loyalty points.
Fix: the transactional outbox. Write the event into an outbox table in the same database transaction as the order; a relay then publishes everything in the outbox to the bus.

callout.text: Either both the order and its event are saved, or neither is. The relay retries until the bus accepts it — so subscribers must handle duplicates. It can poll the table, or tail the database’s own log (change data capture, e.g. Debezium).

changes: + Orders DB with an outbox table
~ No more lost events after a crash

steps.title: Case: replaying history
body: Analytics finds a bug that miscounted revenue for the last 30 days. With a classic queue, those events are gone once consumed.
A log-based bus like Kafka keeps events for days or weeks. Analytics fixes its code, rewinds its position to 30 days ago, and reprocesses every event — other subscribers aren’t affected.

callout.text: Retained events also let a brand-new subscriber build its data from history instead of starting empty.

steps.title: Recap
body:
• Direct calls make the caller slow and fragile, and couple every team to it.
  • Publish an event; every subscriber gets its own copy.
  • New features just subscribe; down subscribers catch up later.
  • Pay for it with eventual consistency, duplicates and harder tracing.
  • Use an outbox so saves and events never disagree; retained logs allow replay.

callout.text: Next up: Real-time Updates — getting events all the way to a user’s screen.
